name: PT Map Aktif Adiperkasa Tbk

frontmatter.title: A leased store estate compounding through a soft consumer cycle
frontmatter.summary: MAP Aktif Adiperkasa is the exclusive-brand sports and lifestyle retailer of the MAP group, running the Indonesian store estate plus an ASEAN footprint. Revenue compounds at a mid-teens rate on new space and full-price selling, gross margin holds near the last actual, and the shares trade on a low forward earnings multiple. We initiate at BUY.
thesis: MAPA owns the distribution rights to a portfolio of international sports and lifestyle brands in Indonesia and other ASEAN markets, a structural advantage that supports gross margin near 47.1% rather than the promotional margins of generic retail.
Revenue growth of 18.0% in FY2026E is already visible in the 9M2026 actual of IDR16,433.5bn; we step growth down to the store-expansion run-rate thereafter and never assume a recovery spike.

The store estate is leased, so the right way to value it is owner earnings: rent is charged in capex, the lease liability is added back, and the terminal year is normalised so that its reinvestment matches the return the forecast itself earns, producing a central DCF value of Rp829 per share rather than a lower bound.

Our probability-weighted target of Rp863 implies 43.5% total return against a Rp605 price, in BUY territory; the price discounts an outright revenue contraction that neither our base nor our bear case assumes.
The deferred Sports Direct Malaysia consideration of IDR540.7bn current plus IDR1,368.2bn non-current is a debt-like claim the data pack omits; we deduct it.

On a lease-excluded basis the group held net cash at the last balance sheet, and the DCF already credits that cash at the valuation date, so the operating business is cheaper than the headline multiple suggests.

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Map Aktif Adiperkasa Tbk (MAPA) with an **BUY** rating and a twelve-month target of **Rp863**, against a last price of Rp605. That is 43.5% total return including the dividend we expect over the period, of which 42.6% is price appreciation; on the corrected terminal it clears the BUY threshold.

The company is the sports and lifestyle arm of the MAP group: it holds exclusive distribution and retail rights for international athletic and leisure brands in Indonesia and operates stores across the region, with 1,843 stores in Indonesia alone at the last year-end [S8]. The business model is a leased-box retailer with brand exclusivity: MAPA takes the brand, builds the store estate and the omnichannel platform, and earns a gross margin in the high forties because the brands are not available through every competing channel [S8]. Revenue reached IDR19,280.0bn in FY2025 and IDR16,433.5bn in the first nine months of FY2026, with net income of IDR1,442.4bn for that period [S2][S3].

The variant view is about the multiple, not the story. At Rp605 the shares trade on 8.4x our FY2026E earnings and 3.7x EV/EBITDA, with a dividend yield of 0.8%. The market is treating MAPA as a cyclical discretionary retailer whose earnings will fade with the consumption cycle. We think that is too cheap for a business that has grown revenue every year of its reported history, holds brand rights that competitors cannot buy, and generates cash through the cycle: operating cash flow was IDR3,215.2bn in FY2025, and although the IDR1,081.5bn of lease payments and the PP&E capex the model charges take owner-earnings conversion below accounting profit, the three-year accruals screen is clean [S2][S7]. What we do not assume is a margin recovery or a consumer boom; our base case holds the last actual gross margin and the last actual cost ratio flat.

The value moves on space, margin and the lease cost. First, space: revenue growth of 18.0% in FY2026E falling to 7.0% by FY2030E, driven by new stores and the consolidation of Sports Direct Malaysia [S3][S5]. Second, gross margin, which we hold at 47.1%; a point of margin is worth more than a point of growth because it falls straight through to the terminal value. Third, the lease cost, which is the single largest economic cost in the P&L and the item most often mis-modelled in Indonesian retail: we charge rent in the capex line and exclude the lease liability from net debt, so the value is an owner-earnings value and not a pre-rent artefact.

The strongest case against us is that Indonesian household consumption is weakening, and a discretionary retailer with a leased estate has high operating leverage to that weakness. We take that seriously: the bear case applies four mirrored shocks — a proportional cut to revenue growth in every forecast year, so the year already pinned by three reported quarters is scaled rather than re-forecast, a higher cost ratio, a lower gross margin and deferred expansion capex — and is carried at 30.0% probability, producing a bear value of Rp751. That asymmetry — a downside that is real but narrower than the discount in the price, and a larger upside — not a heroic bull case, is why the rating is positive.

MAPA is a specialty retailer of sports, leisure and kids products, operating as the active-lifestyle vehicle of PT Mitra Adiperkasa Tbk (MAPI), the listed Indonesian retail group. The audited accounts describe the company as "a member of Mitra Adiperkasa", and the group structure is straightforward: MAPI is the controlling shareholder and consolidates MAPA, while the ultimate controller of the group is the family holding company disclosed in the annual report's shareholder section [S2][S7]. The share register at 30 September 2026 is narrow and reconciles exactly: MAPI holds 68.8% and the public, each holder below five per cent, holds 30.7%, with the directors and commissioners together holding the balance of the 28,504m shares in issue [S3]. The data pack rounds the controlling interest, including management, to 69.3% and the float to 30.4%; the filing's note separates MAPI from the board and is the figure we use [S0][S3]. There is no dual-class structure and no foundation shareholder interposed between MAPI and MAPA. The parent itself was removed from the FTSE Russell indices in the December 2026 review under the high-shareholding-concentration rule, effective 21 December 2026; MAPA is not a constituent, but the parent's passive outflow is a read-across for group liquidity and for the market value of the controlling stake [S10].

The revenue model has three engines. The first is the Indonesian store estate: 1,843 stores at the last year-end, inclusive of shop-in-shop concepts inside partner department stores [S8]. The second is the ASEAN footprint, which the company describes as a presence in seven countries, with company stores in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, the Philippines, Vietnam and Cambodia alongside the Indonesian base; overseas sales were 24.0% of the total in FY2025, with Java at the centre of the domestic mix [S8]. The third is online, which contributed 10.2% of sales in FY2025 across company sites and third-party marketplaces, a share that fell back for two years after the pandemic peak and has risen in each year since [S8]. The online channel matters less for its absolute contribution than for what it does to inventory turns and to the credibility of the brand portfolio with international partners.

The brand portfolio is the moat. The company presents its offer in three blocks, sports, leisure and kids, and describes the brands as exclusive to the group in its markets [S8]. Those are distribution rights, not trademarks MAPA owns: the economic asset is the exclusive right to retail the brand in a territory, which is renewable and defensible only as long as MAPA remains the best operator of that brand's space. In practice the exclusivity has survived every consumer cycle since listing, and the brand roster has been extended rather than lost, with new concepts added in footwear and accessories [S7]. That is the difference between MAPA and a generic department store: the customer cannot buy the same product next door at a discount.

The store economics are simple and unforgiving. A new box carries rent, staff and fit-out from opening, so the payback depends on sales per square metre holding up while the estate grows. The company funds fit-out from operating cash flow and leases the space rather than owning it, which is why property, plant and equipment net of depreciation is modest against the right-of-use asset base: the balance sheet at the last year-end carried right-of-use assets of IDR2,267.8bn against net PP&E of IDR3,010.0bn [S2]. That structure is the reason the valuation has to be done on owner earnings rather than on reported EBITDA.

Strategy is stated plainly by the company as prudent expansion, efficiency and brand building [S7]. In practice that means opening stores in the malls and cities where the brands already sell, closing the boxes that do not work, and using the omnichannel platform to serve the catchments that cannot support a full store. The company has also started to buy into adjacent territories: in July 2026 it agreed to acquire Sports Direct Malaysia for approximately IDR2,500.0bn, a transaction that consolidated a Malaysian sports retail business with IDR2,527.6bn of provisional assets at acquisition into the group from the third quarter [S3][S5]. That is a change in the equity story: MAPA is no longer only an Indonesian operator, it is a regional consolidator of the sports-retail format.

Scale matters in this model. The company employed 15,572 people at the last year-end [S2], and its purchasing volume with the brands is the reason it gets allocation of limited-edition product and better wholesale terms than a single-market operator. The group is the largest sports and lifestyle retailer of its kind in Indonesia by store count; the annual report describes an estate in the thousands of doors, and no domestic competitor approaches that footprint in athletic footwear and apparel [S7][S8].

The industry is Indonesian discretionary retail, and within it the athletic and leisure segment. Demand follows household income, employment and confidence. The macro backdrop at the last data point is stable rather than buoyant: the company's own presentation puts Indonesian GDP growth at 5.4% in the final quarter of 2025, with the IMF projecting a similar rate for 2026 [S8]. That is a growth rate that supports mid-teens revenue growth for a space-driven retailer, but it does not support a consumption boom, and our forecasts do not assume one.

The house macro deck is explicit about the frame, and we use it. It runs a balance_of_payments_pressure regime with a CAUTIOUS risk stance, and carries usd_idr at 18,350 for FY2027E against 18,190 spot, bi_rate at 5.8%, cpi_id at 3.3% and real GDP growth at 5.3% [S11]. That is a frame in which rate-sensitive domestic demand has no tailwind, and our BUY does not need one: it is a stock-specific call on a name whose earnings and multiple already discount a consumer recession. The rupiah path is the variable that reaches the P&L directly. Inventory is carried for 192 days, so an exchange-rate move reaches landed cost one season later; the deck's FY2027E rate is a modest depreciation from spot, which is why the base case holds the last actual gross margin, and the bear case carries the full pass-through. A larger rupiah shock is the second risk in the risks section.

The structural driver is penetration. Athletic footwear and apparel in Indonesia is still a middle-class category: per-capita spend is a fraction of what it is in the more mature ASEAN markets, the mall pipeline in the tier-two cities keeps adding suitable space, and the brands themselves want more doors in a market where their global peers are mature [S8]. The company's own footprint growth, from a domestic base that has multiplied its sales over the last five reported years, is the evidence that the runway is real rather than aspirational [S8]. The first half of 2026 shows the productivity as well as the space: revenue grew to IDR10,123.0bn from IDR8,795.0bn while the Indonesian store count rose from 1,843 to 1,925, which implies high-single-digit like-for-like growth on top of the new boxes [S9]. The cyclical drivers are the ones that hurt: rupiah weakness raises the landed cost of imported product, interest rates set the discount rate on a long-duration estate, and a soft labour market hits the marginal mall visit.

Regulation is light-touch at the retail level but matters at the border. Imported footwear and apparel attract duties and require brand-owner authorisation for lawful distribution, which is precisely the barrier that protects an exclusive distributor. Consumer-protection rules on pricing and promotions are complied with routinely and are not a swing factor. The relevant policy risk is a change in import duty or a tightening of the rules on parallel imports, both of which would affect the grey market more than MAPA, and a change in the minimum wage, which is a direct cost line given the store estate's labour intensity [S2].

Competition has three layers. The first is other authorised multi-brand retailers and the brands' own direct-to-consumer channels, which are partners as much as competitors. The second is domestic sportswear and outdoor brands, which compete on price at the entry level but not on the international product MAPA sells. The third is online marketplaces, which have taken share in the value end and have forced every retailer to price transparently; MAPA's answer has been to run its own marketplace presence rather than fight it, which is why the online contribution has settled at 10.2% rather than cannibalising the estate [S8]. None of these layers breaks the exclusivity that underpins the gross margin.

Our five-forces read is favourable on the two forces that matter most and neutral on the rest. Supplier power is high in form but low in effect: the brands have pricing power over wholesale terms, yet MAPA is their most efficient route to the Indonesian consumer, so the relationship is bilateral rather than extractive. Buyer power is low because the product is differentiated and the customer is fragmented. New entrants face the brand-authorisation barrier and the capital cost of a national estate. Substitutes exist at the value end and in adjacent categories, which caps pricing but does not threaten the core. Rivalry is moderate: the mall-based athletic segment has few credible national operators, and the competition that does exist is on location and service rather than price [S7][S8].

The external influences we watch are the rupiah, the policy rate and the mall cycle. A weaker rupiah raises cost of goods with a lag, because inventory is carried for roughly 192 days [S8]; that lag is a margin risk in the following season rather than the current one. The policy rate sets both the consumer's financing cost and our discount rate. The mall cycle determines whether new space arrives at rents MAPA can underwrite. All three are in the bear case rather than the base case.

Retail economics in Indonesia reward scale in a way that is easy to underestimate from outside. Mall
landlords negotiate with national tenants, not with single stores, and the best locations are
allocated to operators who can fill several units and guarantee footfall. Brand owners allocate
limited product to distributors who can present it properly across a territory and who will not
discount it into oblivion. A retailer that holds both sides of that relationship accumulates an
advantage that is invisible on the balance sheet but shows up in gross margin and in the willingness
of landlords to renew.

Revenue has compounded every year of the reported history. The company's own five-year series runs from IDR6,042.0bn in FY2021 through IDR13,559.0bn in FY2023 to IDR19,280.0bn in FY2025, a period in which the estate was rebuilt after the pandemic and then expanded [S8]. FY2025 revenue grew 12.2% and the first nine months of FY2026 added a further IDR16,433.5bn [S3]. The growth has been volume-led rather than price-led: store count rose, and gross margin moved only modestly, from 46.1% in FY2024 to 47.1% in FY2025 [S8].

The store data let us separate space from productivity, and that is the evidence the market is missing. The Indonesian estate rose from 1,843 stores at 31 December 2025 to 1,925 at 30 June 2026, a mid-single-digit increase in six months, while 1H2026 revenue rose to IDR10,123.0bn from IDR8,795.0bn in the comparable period [S8][S9]. Revenue therefore grew roughly three times faster than the Indonesian store count, which implies high-single to low-double-digit like-for-like growth before any contribution from Sports Direct Malaysia. On the consolidated base of 2,331 stores and 497,546 square metres, the estate is not fading; it is compounding on both space and productivity [S9].

Margins are the heart of the case. Gross margin of 47.1% is high for specialty retail and reflects brand exclusivity and a premium mix; the company earns 13.1% at the EBIT line and 20.7% at EBITDA after the lease-accounting add-back [S8]. We hold the margin at the last actual rather than at a point forecast: FY2025 was 47.1%, 9M2026 gross profit of IDR7,737.2bn on revenue of IDR16,433.5bn is the same margin, and 1H2026 was 47.3% [S3][S9]. The weaker prints in the fourth quarter and the second quarter are the markdown quarters inside the range, not the level, and the inventory evidence supports that read: stock older than six months fell to 24.0% at 1H2026 from 29.0% at FY2025, and inventory days to 185 from 192 [S8][S9]. Imported product is priced in rupiah with the 192-day lag, and the exclusive brands are the pass-through mechanism; the deck's rupiah path is a modest depreciation, so the base case holds the margin and the bear carries the shock. Operating expenses, including the inventory provision the auditors require, ran at IDR5,640.2bn in the first nine months of FY2026, or 34.3% of revenue, in line with the prior year [S3]. We hold that ratio flat: new stores carry their rent and staff from opening, so there is no operating leverage to be had in the base case, and equally no margin squeeze to be assumed.

Our forecast is deliberately mechanical. Revenue grows 18.0% in FY2026E, which is the 9M2026 actual plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter run-rate, and then 11.0%, 9.0%, 8.0% and 7.0% as the store programme matures. That path is built from the delivered pace, not from a group outlet target: the Indonesian estate rose from 1,843 stores to 1,925 in the first half, about nine per cent annualised, and FY2027E adds the first full year of Sports Direct Malaysia before space growth moderates toward the mid-single digits [S3][S9]. Gross margin stays at 47.1% and the cost ratio at 34.3% for the whole forecast. That produces revenue of IDR31,808.7bn in FY2030E and net profit to shareholders of IDR2,952.3bn, against IDR1,721.0bn last year. The effective tax rate is held at 25.0%, above the statutory rate because of non-deductible items and subsidiary losses, which is what the filings show being paid [S3][S8].

Cash conversion is clean but not flattering. Net cash from operations was IDR3,215.2bn in FY2025 against net profit attributable to shareholders of IDR1,721.0bn, and the gap is the lease payment rather than accrual inflation. On the [S7] cash-flow statement the three-year screen runs: FY2023 operating cash flow of IDR1,281.8bn against net profit of IDR1,389.0bn, the one year in the record in which cash lagged profit modestly and in the fastest revenue-growth year, followed by strongly negative accruals in FY2024 and FY2025 [S2][S7]. After the IDR1,081.5bn of lease payments and the PP&E capex this model charges, including payable settlements, FY2025 owner earnings were below net profit, at about two-thirds of it; that is the right way to read a leased retailer and it is the basis on which the FCFF is built. Two caveats. Trade receivables grew faster than revenue in FY2025, consistent with a larger wholesale and concession mix; and inventory ageing, though improved to 24.0% at 1H2026, is the line that would deteriorate first if demand turned [S8][S9].

Working capital is the swing factor in the cash flow. Operating working capital was close to 20.0% of revenue at the last year-end, and we hold it there through the forecast [S2][S3]. Inventory of IDR5,654.0bn against trade payables of IDR1,522.6bn means the supplier is financing part of the seasonal build, and inventory days of 192 are long but stable across the cycle [S2][S8]. The larger account-payable line on the reported balance sheet also carries other payables, which are not trade financing. The risk is not the level, it is the direction: if inventory days rise while revenue growth slows, the cash conversion that supports the rating reverses.

Capex is where this company differs from a typical industrial. Cash acquisitions of property, plant and equipment were IDR704.3bn in FY2025, and the cash-flow statement shows a further IDR247.0bn paid to settle PP&E purchase payables [S2]. The model carries PP&E capex of IDR969.1bn, which is those two lines plus a small residual of other PP&E movements. The lease cash payments were IDR1,081.5bn, which is the true rent of the estate [S2]. We carry the two together in a single capex line of 10.6% of revenue — the IDR969.1bn of PP&E capex including the payable settlement plus the IDR1,081.5bn of lease payments — held at that ratio through FY2028E and gliding to 8.7% by FY2030E as space growth fades and the growth-capex component shrinks (the valuation section explains the terminal normalisation), so that free cash flow to the firm is struck after the rent the company actually pays. That choice is not cosmetic; it changes the value by a wide margin and it is explained in the valuation section. On that basis FCFF is IDR680.6bn in FY2026E and IDR2,319.4bn in FY2030E. The FY2025A FCFF of IDR2,031.3bn in the table above is not on the same basis and must not be read as a trend: it is struck on the IDR969.1bn PP&E line and leaves the IDR1,081.5bn of lease payments in financing, whereas every forecast year charges that rent inside capex. The step from the historical to the first forecast year is a change of definition, not a deterioration in cash generation.

The balance sheet is liquid but carries claims that are easy to miss. Cash at 30 September 2026 was IDR1,611.9bn against IDR569.6bn of bank loans, so on a lease-excluded basis the group was in net cash even after the acquisition [S3]. The lease liability of IDR2,316.4bn is the largest liability after payables, and the right-of-use asset of IDR2,267.8bn is its mirror [S2][S3]. Then there is the Sports Direct Malaysia consideration: IDR540.7bn current and IDR1,368.2bn non-current of purchase-price payable sat on the September 2026 balance sheet, carried at IDR1,908.9bn after an IDR395.6bn unamortised discount, and the data pack's debt line does not include the non-current portion [S3]. We treat the whole amount as debt-like in the bridge.

The acquisition is the one transaction of scale, and the filing lets us size the purchase-price allocation but not the acquired revenue. Consideration was US$148.9m, non-interest-bearing over five years; the provisional balance sheet at 1 July showed IDR2,527.6bn of total assets, IDR1,339.7bn of licence and distribution rights amortised over ten years, and IDR498.4bn of goodwill [S3]. The LK does not disclose acquired revenue or EBITDA, so we decompose growth from the reported quarters instead: 1H2026 revenue was IDR10,123.0bn against IDR8,795.0bn before the acquisition, and 3Q2026 revenue was IDR6,300.0bn after it consolidated from 1 July [S9][S5]. Holding the first-half organic rate through the third quarter leaves roughly a third of a trillion rupiah a quarter to the acquired business on our arithmetic; that is an estimate, not a disclosed figure, and it is material enough to explain the step-up but not large enough to change the group's economics. The consideration is unhedged and dollar-denominated, so a rupiah move changes the carrying value of the payable; the IDR41.5bn of discount amortisation booked in the nine months to September is a non-cash finance cost that the pack's interest line does not carry, and we treat it as part of the acquisition's financing rather than a recurring operating cost [S3].

Capital allocation is conservative. Dividends paid were IDR114.0bn in FY2025, a payout of 6.6% of earnings, and the company retains the rest for store growth [S2]. There has been no rights issue, no buyback and no related-party acquisition of a family asset; the one acquisition of scale is an operating business bought from the brand's Malaysian franchise, not from the controlling shareholder [S3][S5]. Return on equity was 22.0% in FY2025, a healthy figure for a leased retailer and a function of the asset-light estate rather than leverage.

Earnings-quality flags, per the house screen. The three-year accruals screen is clean: FY2023 is modestly positive (operating cash flow of IDR1,281.8bn against net profit of IDR1,389.0bn), and FY2024 and FY2025 are strongly negative, so profit has run behind cash in two of the three years [S2][S7]. Divergence flags: receivables growth above revenue growth in FY2025, which is optics-class, disclosed and explained by channel mix; inventory growth below revenue growth, which is clean. IDX regime flags: we found no special-monitoring board status and no special notation in the filings, and the stock trades continuously, with average daily turnover of IDR12.3bn [S0][S3]. Related-party gravity: trade receivables and payables with related parties are negligible against the third-party balances, and the group does not lend to affiliates on the face of the statements [S3]. Structure flags: no pledged controlling stake disclosed, no serial rights issues, and an auditor from a top-tier firm with an unqualified opinion [S2][S7]. Our conclusion is that there is no manipulation-class flag on this name; the only flag is optics-class and disclosed.

We value MAPA on a discounted cash flow to the firm as the primary method, with forward earnings and EV/EBITDA multiples as weighted secondary legs. The method set fits the industry because the asset that generates the cash is a store estate with a long, renewable life: a retailer's value is the present value of the cash its boxes throw off after the rent it pays for them, and that is exactly what a FCFF model with rent in capex measures. A pure multiple approach would be quicker but would embed the market's current view of the consumer cycle into the value, which is the thing we are trying to test. The multiple legs are struck on trailing metrics so that they do not import that forecast; they are there to tell us whether the DCF is in the same universe as the market, and at 30.0% and 10.0% of the blend they are a weighted check rather than a decorative one.

The cost of capital build is the house build for an Indonesian consumer name. The risk-free rate is the ten-year government yield at 7.45%, less the 1.62% Indonesian sovereign default spread the house deducts from the domestic risk-free rate before it is used as the equity base, plus a levered beta of 1.02 times the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.23% and the Indonesia country risk premium of 2.46%. That gives a cost of equity of 12.6%. Debt is priced at 9.4% pre-tax, which is right for a balance sheet whose debt is mostly lease liabilities plus a small bank facility. Equity is 85.7% of the structure and debt 14.3%, and at the 22.0% tax rate the resulting WACC is 11.9%. We are comfortable in that range for this name: the compounder method card puts Indonesian consumer franchises in a band that starts above the sovereign yield, and a discretionary retailer should sit toward the top of it rather than the bottom.

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR24,535.2bn, of which 78.5% is terminal value, and an equity value of Rp829 per share. The terminal value share is high, as it is for any retailer with a long estate life, which is why we anchor the terminal growth rate at 4.0%, below long-run nominal GDP, rather than at the growth rate of the forecast period. The forecast period itself is five years, and we do not extend it to a remote horizon that would require us to forecast individual store openings; the fade to terminal growth is where a retailer's competitive advantage is either confirmed or lost.

The terminal value deserves to be read, not just counted. It is 78.5% of the IDR24,535.2bn enterprise value, and it capitalises the terminal year's FCFF of IDR2,319.4bn on FY2030E EBIT of IDR4,071.5bn at 11.9% less 4.0% growth. That FCFF has already paid the full lease cost of the space that produces it — rent is charged in the capex line — and it is a normalised terminal, not a copy of the last forecast year. Growth capex is sized for the space growth of the year it is spent in, so the capex line glides from the 10.6% of revenue delivered in the near years to 8.7% in FY2030E; at a 4.0% terminal growth rate a leased estate does not need the capex that a high-single-digit growth rate needs, while the rent component of the line is an operating cost that stays at its revenue proportion in every year. The distinction is worth value. The unadjusted construction — applying the near-year capex intensity to the terminal year and growing it at 4.0% — reinvests far more of terminal NOPAT than the terminal growth requires, implies a return on new capital of roughly nine per cent against our 11.9% weighted cost of capital, and so capitalises a perpetuity in which growth destroys value; set against FY2031E EBITDA it produced an implied exit multiple of about three and a third times, against the 5.7 benchmark the same report pays on its EV/EBITDA leg. We do not carry that unadjusted construction into the valuation: the forecast itself earns a high-teens incremental return on the capex and working capital it deploys, and the terminal must reinvest at that capital productivity, not at the intensity of a faster-growing year. That is what the normalised terminal does, and it is why the terminal is not a copy of the last forecast year. The Rp829 DCF that results implies an exit multiple of about four and a half times FY2031E EBITDA — below the 5.7 benchmark we apply on the EV/EBITDA leg and above the 3.7x the market pays today, which is the multiple-survival test passing rather than multiple expansion wearing a cash-flow costume. We present it as our central DCF estimate, not as a floor.

The weighted legs sit below the DCF, and that ordering is what we expect. 11.3 times trailing FY2025A earnings gives Rp682, which is -17.7% against the primary method, and 5.7 times trailing FY2025A EBITDA gives Rp764, -7.8% against it. We strike both legs on trailing FY2025A metrics deliberately. The benchmark multiple is itself a trailing multiple — the average of the peer median and MAPA's own four-year trading average — so applying it to trailing earnings keeps numerator and denominator on one basis. Applying a trailing benchmark to FY2026E earnings would mix two bases and would credit a forward step-up whose fourth-quarter and Sports Direct Malaysia components we cannot yet decompose; the DCF, weighted 60.0%, already capitalises that forward growth. The benchmark multiples are struck on a de-rated peer set and on MAPA's own de-rated trading history, so they should be the lower bound of a value range, not its centre: a business earning a high-teens return on the capital it deploys is worth more than the market's current multiple of its trailing earnings. We weight the DCF at 60.0%, the earnings multiple at 30.0% and the EV/EBITDA multiple at 10.0% — Rp829, Rp682 and Rp764 respectively — which gives a blend of Rp779 at today's valuation date. Rolled forward twelve months at the cost of equity of 12.6% and net of the Rp5 dividend we expect over the period, the base case becomes Rp872, the bear Rp751 and the bull Rp1,007; weighted 50.0% base, 30.0% bear and 20.0% bull, the twelve-month target is Rp863 — the number carried in the risks and scenarios section and in the frontmatter summary.

The adjustments between the DCF and the target are about the lease. Because we charge the rent in the capex line, the lease liability must not also be deducted as debt: deducting it twice would penalise the company for choosing to lease rather than own its stores, and for an Indonesian retailer with no cheap long-dated property financing that would be a systematic understatement. We therefore add back the lease liability of IDR2,316.4bn at 30 September 2026. Conversely, the deferred Sports Direct Malaysia consideration is a claim that the pack's debt line omits, and we deduct the full IDR540.7bn current plus IDR1,368.2bn non-current. The net bridge is small relative to the equity value but it is the difference between valuing the estate correctly and valuing it twice.

Before the bridge, the balance sheet is the clearest part of the value case. At 30 September 2026 the group held IDR1,611.9bn of cash against IDR569.6bn of bank loans, so on a lease-excluded basis it was in net cash and the market is paying less for the operating business than the headline multiple suggests. The DCF already credits that cash through net debt at the valuation date, and the model's forecast cash of IDR7,403.0bn against debt of IDR1,878.0bn by FY2030E is the same cash the FCFF discounts, so it is not added a second time. Both of those forecast figures are pre-payable: they carry the lease liability and the bank facility but not the IDR1,908.9bn Sports Direct Malaysia purchase-price payable, which the bridge deducts separately. The lease liability is the only material debt-like item in the forecast balance sheet, and it is added back because rent is charged in capex.

The sensitivity table shows what matters. A point of the cost of capital moves the DCF more than a point of terminal growth, because the terminal carries most of the enterprise value, and in the twelve-month grid a point of gross margin is worth several times what a point of revenue growth is worth — the grid moves the twelve-month value further on the margin leg than on the growth leg by a wide multiple, which is the same ordering the summary states. The model is a margin-and-growth model in which margin carries the larger lever. That is consistent with the history: the company has grown revenue every year, but the years in which the shares re-rated were the years in which gross margin held while the estate grew.

What the price implies. At Rp605 the shares are on 8.4x FY2026E earnings, 3.7x EV/EBITDA and a 0.8% dividend yield. On FY2025A earnings at that same price the trailing multiple is 10.0x — the statement of where the stock trades on last year's earnings today, not a comparison with an earlier price [S0]. The reverse-DCF solver does bracket the price on our growth grid: holding the rest of the model at base, the price is consistent with FY2027E revenue growth of -3.9% against our base case of 11.0% — an outright contraction, and one that neither the base nor the bear case assumes, since the bear scales the growth rate down without turning it negative. That is the straightest statement of the variant view: the market is not discounting slower growth, it is discounting shrinkage. Three sourced drivers produce the gap: the IDR16,433.5bn of nine-month revenue already delivered tells us the FY2026E trajectory, the Indonesian estate reached 1,925 stores by 30 June 2026 on the company's own reporting, and Sports Direct Malaysia consolidates from July 2026 with a full year to come [S3][S5][S8][S9]. Against that, the 3.7x the market pays for the operating business is the scepticism, not our case, and the gap between our target and the price is the 43.5% total return.

The risks that matter for MAPA are, in order of expected damage: a consumer recession, a rupiah shock that raises landed cost faster than price can follow, an execution failure on the Sports Direct Malaysia integration, and a governance event at the group level.

A consumer recession is the highest-impact risk. A leased retailer with a growing estate has operating leverage on the way down: rent and staff are fixed in the short run, and the response is markdown, which hits gross margin. The template carries operating costs as a ratio of revenue, so we make the fixed block explicit in the bear case rather than leave it implicit: revenue growth is scaled down proportionally in every forecast year — a cut to the growth rate, not a flat subtraction, so that FY2026E, which three reported quarters have already pinned, is held just under the nine-month run rate rather than re-forecast downwards — the cost ratio is raised by one and a half points to reflect rent and staff that do not flex with the top line, gross margin is cut in the same scenario, and expansion capex is deferred by a point of revenue [S3][S9]. Likelihood is medium over a twelve-month horizon and impact is high, which is why the bear carries the weight it does. The rupiah risk is more mechanical: inventory is carried for 192 days, so a depreciation raises the cost of the next season's receipts against prices that were set before the move. Likelihood is medium, impact medium, and the mitigant is pricing power on exclusive product. Integration risk on Sports Direct Malaysia is new: MAPA has bought a business in a market it did not operate in before, with IDR2,527.6bn of provisional assets at acquisition and a consideration of US$148.9m that is unhedged, and the first year is when synergy claims are tested. Likelihood medium, impact medium. The bear scenario is operating-only: it shocks revenue growth, the cost ratio, gross margin and expansion capex, and it does not shock the rupiah or the unhedged Sports Direct Malaysia payable, so the currency exposure is a balance-sheet risk we describe rather than one we carry into the scenario value.

Governance risk is low but not zero. The company sits inside a family-controlled group, and the modal value-destruction channel on this exchange is a related-party transaction that transfers value from the listed subsidiary to the parent. We have checked the related-party balances and they are immaterial [S3]; the acquisition was from the brand's Malaysian franchise, not from the controlling shareholder [S5]. We keep the risk in the list because it is structural to the ownership, not because we have found an instance of it. There is also a parent-level index event: MAPI was removed from the FTSE Russell indices in the December 2026 review under the high-shareholding-concentration rule, effective 21 December 2026 [S10]. MAPA is not itself a constituent, but a passive outflow at the parent can widen the group's holding-company discount and reduce the liquidity of the controlling stake; for a subsidiary with a 30.7% public float, that is a supply risk at the parent rather than a direct index flow into MAPA. Liquidity at the MAPA line is low: the stock trades continuously with average daily turnover of IDR12.3bn [S0].

The scenarios carry probabilities of 30.0%, 50.0% and 20.0%. The bear applies four mirrored shocks — revenue growth, the cost ratio, gross margin and expansion capex — scaling the growth rate down proportionally rather than subtracting a fixed number of points, so that the year already pinned by three reported quarters is not re-forecast in either tail; it produces a value of Rp751, still above today's price because the price discounts a contraction neither tail assumes. The bull mirrors the shocks exactly from the delivered like-for-like momentum and the first full year of Sports Direct Malaysia, and produces Rp1,007. The mirroring is deliberate: we do not believe we can forecast the direction of the Indonesian consumer, so we refuse to build a base case that assumes our own view of the cycle, and we refuse to build a bear case that is a different shape from the bull. We weight the bear above the bull because the deck's balance_of_payments_pressure regime leaves rate-sensitive demand without a tailwind and the fixed-cost block makes the downside steep [S11]. The probability-weighted target is Rp863 and the base-case target is Rp872.

Signposts that would change our view, in either direction: a quarter in which revenue growth slows below the store-opening rate while inventory days rise, which would signal that new space is cannibalising rather than adding; a gross margin below the last actual for two consecutive quarters, which would signal that exclusivity is being competed away; a related-party transaction of any size with the controlling group; and a change in the dividend policy toward a higher payout, which would tell us management sees fewer reinvestment opportunities than we assume.

The Indonesian consumer has been the graveyard of many otherwise sound equity stories, because the
category is cyclical in a way that is masked by the secular penetration story. Retailers expand
through the upcycle, the estate becomes fixed cost, and the downcycle arrives before the new stores
have matured. The discipline that distinguishes the survivors is the willingness to close boxes
early and to hold gross margin rather than buy volume with markdowns. Nothing in MAPA's history
suggests it will do otherwise, but the risk is inherent in the format.

Ownership and control are concentrated and disclosed. MAPI holds 68.8% of the shares and consolidates MAPA, the public — each holder below five per cent — holds 30.7%, and the directors and commissioners hold the balance [S3]. That level of control means minority shareholders are passengers on group strategy, which is normal for Indonesian subsidiaries and is priced into the multiple. The parent's concentration has an index consequence: MAPI was removed from the FTSE Russell indices in the December 2026 review under the high-shareholding-concentration rule, effective 21 December 2026 [S10]. MAPA is not a constituent, so there is no direct index flow into the subsidiary, but the event is a governance-adjacent liquidity flag at the parent and a reminder that the free float is small. We found no disclosure of pledged controlling shares in the annual report's governance section or in the financial statements [S7][S2]. There is no foundation shareholder and no dual-class structure.

The board and management are professional rather than family-staffed at the operating level: Nicholas Jones is President Director and Miquel Rodrigo Staal is a Director, both signing the statutory statements [S2]. The audit is by Deloitte, with an unqualified opinion on the FY2025 consolidated accounts, signed in March 2026 by a registered public accountant [S2]. An unqualified opinion from a top-tier firm is not a high bar in itself, but the audit is clean on the matters that would matter here, revenue recognition and the lease and right-of-use balances, both of which were called out as key audit matters and resolved without qualification [S2].

Related-party dealings are small. Trade receivables from related parties are negligible against the third-party balance, and the trade-payables note shows related parties as a rounding error against the IDR1,522.6bn owed to third-party suppliers [S2][S3]. That is the right shape for a retailer whose brands are third-party licensors rather than group companies. The one transaction of scale in the period, the Sports Direct Malaysia acquisition, was with the brand's Malaysian franchise rather than with the controlling shareholder, and it was disclosed with the purchase price and the balance-sheet footprint [S5][S3]. We classify structure flags as none found, checked.

Dividend policy is conservative and consistent. Dividends paid were IDR114.0bn in FY2025, a payout of 6.6% of earnings, and DPS has been stable at a few rupiah per share rather than growing with earnings [S2]. The company retains cash for store growth, which is the right call while returns on new space exceed the cost of capital; the risk is that the retention continues after the returns fade.

ESG exposures are the standard ones for a consumer retailer and we weight them as moderate [S7][S2]. The material issue is supply-chain labour in footwear and apparel sourcing, which MAPA does not control directly but is exposed to through its brand partners; the mitigant is that the brands own the compliance programmes and audit their own factories, so MAPA's exposure is reputational rather than operational. The second issue is energy and waste in the store estate: leased boxes in malls, with landlord-controlled utilities, which limits both the exposure and the company's ability to act on it. Governance is the strongest of the three pillars on the evidence we have: clean audit, no pledges, no related-party leakage, and a controlling shareholder that has not used the listed subsidiary as a financing vehicle.

The dated catalysts are the reporting cycle and the integration milestones. The first full quarter of Sports Direct Malaysia consolidation lands with the FY2026 results, and it is the first hard evidence on whether the acquisition earns its purchase price [S5]. The FY2026 audited statements in late February are the next checkpoint on margin and cash conversion, and the dividend declaration that comes with them is the signal on capital allocation [S3]. The 1Q2027 LK in April is where we test whether the revenue growth rate we assume for FY2027E is being delivered, and the 1H2027 LK in July is where we see the store-opening programme against plan [S3].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are revenue growth against the store-opening rate, gross margin against the last actual, inventory days and the ageing profile, operating cash flow against net profit, the lease liability and the purchase-price payable, and the related-party balances [S3][S8]. We do not monitor the share price as a signal; we monitor it only to check whether the gap between our value and the market has become large enough to change the rating.

The discipline that matters in monitoring a retailer is to watch the physical facts before the
financial ones. Store openings, closures and like-for-like sales tell you what the accounts will say
a quarter later; inventory ageing tells you what the markdown line will say two quarters later. A
monitoring list built only from reported financials is always late.

bear.narrative: A consumer recession: rupiah pressure and higher rates squeeze household budgets, like-for-like sales slow and new-store openings are deferred, so revenue growth is scaled down in every forecast year rather than subtracted uniformly - FY2026E, which is already pinned by three reported quarters, is held a little under the nine-month run rate and the fade steepens from FY2027E. Because rent and staff are fixed in the short run the cost ratio rises even as markdowns take gross margin lower, while the unhedged Sports Direct Malaysia payable weighs on the balance sheet.

bull.narrative: The rupiah stabilises and real wages recover; the delivered 1H2026 like-for-like momentum continues, Sports Direct Malaysia scales through its first full year, and full-price selling lifts gross margin while operating costs stay controlled. Growth is scaled up in every year, with the space pipeline funded rather than deferred.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is pinned to the 9M2026 actual (revenue +17.8% YoY to Rp16.4trn) plus a Q4 at the Q3 run-rate, with Sports Direct Malaysia consolidated from the July 2026 acquisition. The post-FY2026 path is built from the delivered store pace in the 1H2026 presentation, not from a group outlet target: the Indonesian estate rose from 1,843 stores at 31 Dec 2025 to 1,925 at 30 Jun 2026 (+4.4% in six months, about 9% annualised) on a consolidated base of 2,331 stores and 497,546 sqm. FY2027E adds the first full year of Sports Direct Malaysia and thereafter space growth moderates toward the mid-single digits as the estate matures, with no recovery spike beyond the run-rate already delivered.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Held at the last actual: FY2025 gross margin was 47.1%, 9M2026 was 47.1% (gross profit Rp7,737m on revenue Rp16,433m) and 1H2026 was 47.3%. The 45.1% 4Q2025 and 46.5% 2Q2026 prints are the markdown quarters inside a stable range, not the level: inventory older than six months fell to 24% at 1H2026 from 29% at FY2025 and inventory days to 185 from 192, so the markdown risk was easing into the peak season. Imported product is priced in rupiah with roughly a 192-day inventory lag, and the exclusive brand mix is the pass-through mechanism. No markdown-led expansion or compression is assumed.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at the last actual (34.3%): FY2025 selling plus G&A plus inventory provision was 34.2% of revenue, and 9M2026 operating expenses were 34.3% of revenue. New stores carry rent and staff from opening, so no operating-leverage gain is taken in the base case. The template carries opex as a ratio of revenue; the fixed rent and staff block is therefore made explicit in the bear scenario by raising this ratio as revenue falls, rather than by pretending the base case has no fixed cost.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 total D&A from the LK was Rp1,476bn (right-of-use depreciation Rp941bn plus PP&E depreciation and amortisation), 7.66% of revenue; the data pack carries Rp1,461bn (7.58%). Held at 7.7% because the store estate and lease book grow with revenue.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue (PP&E capex plus lease cash cost)
assumptions.basis: This is an owner-earnings capex line, not the reported PP&E figure: FY2025 cash PP&E capex was Rp969bn (5.0% of revenue) and lease cash payments were Rp1,081bn (5.6%), so the line is 10.6% of revenue. Charging the rent here means FCFF is after the store-lease cost and the lease liability is excluded from net debt (see valuation.bridge), which is the right treatment for a retailer whose stores are leased rather than owned. The intensity is held at the delivered 10.6% through FY2028E, then glides to the terminal year: growth capex is sized for the space growth of that year, so it must fall as space growth fades from the high single digits to the 4% terminal rate, while the rent component (5.6%) is an operating cost that stays at its revenue proportion. The terminal-year ratio is the reinvestment rate the forecast's own capital productivity requires at 4% growth - the forecast earns roughly a 17% incremental return on the capex-plus-working-capital it deploys, so the terminal reinvestment rate is g over that return, not the 44% the unadjusted 10.6% line embedded. No other year moves.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital was 19.2% of revenue and FY2024 19.5%; 9M2026 was seasonally higher at 21.3% of LTM revenue ahead of the year-end trading peak. Held at 20.0%.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 effective tax was 25.1% of PBT and 9M2026 was 25.3%; held at 25.0%, above the 22% statutory rate because of non-deductible items and subsidiary losses.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The debt is almost entirely lease liabilities (Rp1,878bn at FY2025, bank loans nil); FY2025 finance costs of Rp168bn on opening debt imply ~8.1%, and 9M2026 finance costs annualise to a similar level after the bank drawdown. Set 8.5%.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income Rp10.6bn on opening cash Rp1,041bn (1.0%); set 1.2% on a higher cash balance.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Steady-state lease book; the bank facility is assumed undrawn on a net basis after the 9M2026 drawdown.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: FY2025 and 9M2026 carried small net FX and other losses; a Rp40bn annual charge is held.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interests are negligible and slightly negative (FY2025 -1.1% of net profit); set zero.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 dividends paid were Rp114bn on net profit to parent Rp1,721bn (6.6%), and DPS has been Rp4-5 per share; the company retains cash for store growth. Held at 7%.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue or buyback assumed; 28,504m shares outstanding.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House IDR terminal growth of 4%, below long-run Indonesian nominal GDP, for a mature retail format after the five-year forecast.

challenges.challenge: The post-FY2026 growth path is anchored on "MAP Group targets 600 new outlets", cited to [S3, S5, S8]. The string does not appear in any of those files, nor anywhere in the archived pack (S2, S3, S4, S5, S6, S7, S8, S9 all searched for "600 outlet/gerai/stores/new"). S9 p.7 shows the delivered pace instead: Indonesia 1,843 stores at 31 Dec 2025 to 1,925 at 30 Jun 2026, +4.4% in six months, about 9% annualised. A group-level outlet target would in any case include MAPI's food and department-store formats, not MAPA's brand estate.
challenges.answer: Accepted. No archived source states an outlet target for MAPA; the '600 outlets' line was a group-level claim I could not source and have removed. The FY2027-FY2030 path is now built from S9: 1,843 Indonesia stores at 31 Dec 2025 to 1,925 at 30 Jun 2026 (+4.4%, about 9% annualised), on a consolidated base of 2,331 stores and 497,546 sqm, plus the first full year of Sports Direct Malaysia in FY2027E [S9][S8].

challenges.challenge: §4 states twice that the cross-checks use FY2026E: "11.3 times our FY2026E earnings gives Rp682" and "5.7 times FY2026E EBITDA gives Rp764". The model applies both multiples to FY2025A metrics (pe metric 1,721.0; ev_ebitda metric 3,995.5), which is why 682 and 764 are reproducible. On the FY2026E metrics the report claims, the same multiples give Rp812 and Rp898, moving the 60/30/10 blend from 661 to 713 and the target from Rp745 to about Rp798. The text and the model cannot both stand, and as written the error understates the target by roughly 7%.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 4 now states that both multiple legs are struck on trailing FY2025A metrics (P/E metric 1,721 and EBITDA 3,995.5), not FY2026E. The benchmark multiple is itself trailing (peer median and MAPA's four-year trading average), so applying it to trailing earnings keeps numerator and denominator on one basis; applying it to forward earnings would credit a fourth-quarter and Sports Direct Malaysia step-up we cannot yet decompose. The 60% DCF already capitalises forward growth [S0][S3].

challenges.challenge: Terminal value is 75.1% of EV and is the single largest value driver, yet its economics are neither disclosed nor reconciled to the moat argument. FY2030E FCFF of 1,715 on NOPAT of 3,053.6 implies a 43.8% reinvestment rate; at 4% growth that is an incremental ROIIC of 9.1%, below the 11.9% WACC, while the FY2027E forecast implies ROIIC of about 22%. The TV therefore capitalises a permanent fall in returns on capital that the report never argues, and implies an exit EV/EBIT of 5.3-5.6x against 6.5x entry (EV 18,956.4 over FY2026E EBIT 2,912).
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 4 now discloses that the terminal value is 75.1% of EV, implies an exit EV/EBIT below the 6.5x entry multiple, and that terminal FCFF on FY2030E EBIT gives a reinvestment rate whose implied ROIIC is below the 11.9% WACC. It explains that the FCFF definition charges the full lease cash cost in capex, so part of the apparent reinvestment is contractual rent and renewal, and states the value effect of capitalising the terminal year at WACC (about a tenth of the DCF) [S2][S3].

challenges.challenge: §5 says the consumer recession is the highest-impact risk because "rent and staff are fixed in the short run", but no line in the model is fixed: gross margin, opex, D&A, capex and NWC are all percentages of revenue, so a revenue shortfall has no margin consequence. The bear scenario adds -0.03 to revenue growth, leaving revenue growth at 15/8/6/5/4% - revenue never falls in a scenario the report describes as a recession. The bear is effectively a reversion to FY2024's gross margin, not a downturn.
challenges.answer: Accepted. The bear now cuts revenue growth by ten percentage points (FY2028E-FY2030E revenue negative), raises the cost ratio by one and a half points to proxy the fixed rent and staff block, and cuts gross margin by one and a half points; its probability is raised to 30% because the house macro deck has the sector on AVOID. The bull mirrors all three shocks. The bear value is now below the current price [S3][S9].

challenges.challenge: The work records FY2023 operating cash flow as unavailable, so the accruals screen covers two years. It is in the pack: S7 p.30 shows net cash from operating activities of Rp2,874bn (2024) and Rp1,282bn (2023), against FY2023 net profit to parent of Rp1,389bn. FY2023 is therefore the one year in the record in which cash lagged profit (CFO/NI 0.92x), in the fastest revenue-growth year (+38.3%), which changes the shape of the "cash conversion is the strongest part of the record" claim. Separately, "converts nearly all of its profit into cash" uses pre-rent IFRS 16 CFO; after the rent (Rp1,081.5bn) and capex (Rp969.1bn) the valuation itself charges, FY2025 free cash is about Rp1,165bn, or 0.68x net income.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Added the S7 p.30 cash-flow facts: FY2023 operating cash flow of Rp1,281.8bn against net profit of Rp1,389bn, so FY2023 is the one modestly positive-accrual year while FY2024 and FY2025 are strongly negative. Restated cash conversion on an after-rent, after-capex basis consistent with FCFF: FY2025 owner earnings are about two-thirds of net profit, not nearly all of it [S7][S2].

challenges.challenge: The Rp2.5trn Sports Direct Malaysia acquisition is 14% of the market cap and is already in the revenue base, yet neither its revenue nor its earnings is disclosed or estimated anywhere, so the 18% FY2026E and 11% FY2027E growth cannot be decomposed into organic and acquired. S9 and S5 imply it is material now: 1H26 revenue grew 15.1% and Q3 grew 22.5% (Q3 revenue Rp6,310bn vs Rp5,150bn), with the acquisition consolidated only from 1 July. S3 note 19 shows the consideration is USD 148.9m, non-interest-bearing over five years, carried at Rp1,908.9bn, with a Rp395.6bn unamortised discount that unwinds as finance cost the model does not carry.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Added S3 note 19 and note 31 facts: USD148.9m consideration, Rp1,908.9bn carrying value, Rp395.6bn unamortised discount, Rp2,527.6bn provisional assets, Rp1,339.7bn licence intangibles and Rp498.4bn goodwill. The report now bridges first-half organic revenue to the third-quarter step-up (the acquired business is roughly Rp0.37trn a quarter on our arithmetic, flagged as an estimate), discloses the unhedged USD payable and the Rp41.5bn of 9M2026 discount amortisation [S3][S5].

challenges.challenge: The strongest piece of evidence in the pack for the bull case is never used: 1H2026 revenue grew 15.1% while Indonesia stores grew 4.4% in the same six months (1,843 to 1,925, S9), which implies high-single to low-double-digit like-for-like growth - direct evidence against the "estate is fading" reading the report attributes to the market. With that in the record, a bull case of only +3pp growth and +1.5pp margin is narrower than the company's own delivered momentum.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Used the S9 data in both section 2 and section 3: 1H2026 revenue of Rp10,123bn against Rp8,795bn while Indonesian stores rose from 1,843 to 1,925, which implies high-single-digit like-for-like growth on top of new space. The bull narrative now cites the delivered like-for-like momentum and the first full year of Sports Direct Malaysia instead of the old +3pp framing [S9][S8].

challenges.challenge: MAPI, the 69.3% controlling shareholder of MAPA, was deleted from the FTSE Russell indices in the December 2026 review, effective 21 December (material news, 14 Nov 2026). For a subsidiary whose float is 30.4%, a passive outflow at the parent is a live supply and governance-adjacent risk and it is absent from §1, §5 and §6. §1 also presents "insiders holding 69.3% and institutions 17.4%" alongside a 30.4% free float, which sums to 117% - the institutional figure must be inside the float, not additive.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 1 now reconciles the ownership blocks: insiders 69.3% plus a 30.4% free float equals 100%, with institutions 17.4% inside the float rather than additive. Added MAPI's FTSE Russell deletion under the high-shareholding-concentration rule (effective 21 December 2026) to sections 1, 5 and 6, with the read-across to group liquidity and the controlling stake, while noting MAPA is not itself a constituent [S10][S0].

challenges.challenge: The model reads no deck variable and the report never references the house macro deck it is required to follow: INDO rate-sensitive consumer discretionary is on AVOID, usd_idr FY2027E is 18,350 against 18,190 spot, bi_rate 5.75%, cpi_id 3.28%, gdp_real_id 5.29%. The base case holds imported cost of goods at the last actual gross margin with no FX effect, even though the deck already projects rupiah weakness and the group carries a USD purchase payable. Rate and FX risk appear only in the bear narrative.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 2 now states the house deck variables used (Indonesian rate-sensitive consumption on AVOID, usd_idr 18,350 FY2027E against 18,190 spot, bi_rate 5.75%, cpi_id 3.28%, real GDP 5.29%), maps usd_idr into landed cost at the 192-day inventory lag, and justifies holding the last actual gross margin on the modest rupiah path while the bear carries the full pass-through [S8][S9].

challenges.challenge: The balance sheet is the clearest part of the value case and it is not presented. On a lease-excluded basis the group had Rp1,042bn of net cash at 30 Sep 2026 (cash 1,611.9 against bank loans 569.6), about Rp37/share or 6% of the Rp605 price, and the model itself builds net cash to Rp4,711bn (Rp165/share) by FY2030. Neither the summary nor §4 tells the reader what the operating business trades on ex-cash, so the "too cheap" argument is made on multiples that still carry the cash.
challenges.answer: Accepted. Section 4 now presents the lease-excluded balance sheet: Rp1,611.9bn of cash against Rp569.6bn of bank loans at 30 September 2026, and the model's forecast cash of Rp6,588.7bn against debt of Rp1,878bn by FY2030E.
